fields.sections.0.exchanges.1.con.words: Joshua Bowen argues that treating biblical narratives as divine commands while recasting troubling laws as nonlegislative propaganda is interpretively inconsistent and weakens the moral defense.
fields.sections.0.exchanges.1.con.critique: Strongest feature: Bowen exposes selective authority: a defender who trusts the narrative concerning Canaanites, Exodus, and Sinai cannot invoke comparative ancient-law scholarship only when morally troubling commands require neutralization. Principal limitation: his inspiration-versus-propaganda contrast is unnecessarily rigid, because inspiration might operate through historically situated nonlegislative genres, while his assertions about scholarly consensus, Exodus, and Canaanites remain undemonstrated here. Live burden: Bowen must specify which interpretive commitment makes such a layered account incoherent and establish why genre-sensitive accommodation cannot preserve narrative authority without transforming every legal provision into an ideal command. Locked score: 78 rewards exceptional responsiveness, central relevance, and an intelligible consistency objection, but reserves stronger credit because the evidentiary claims are asserted, the alternatives conflate genre with historicity, and the framing insufficiently accommodates a principled mixed interpretation.
